messages.subject: mclapply with nimble
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm wondering if anyone has any recommendations for parallelizing multiple nimble fits? I have been using mclapply() across 50 cores and it has been working okay with small numbers of iterations but some fits fail to load shared libraries when the number of iterations is high. I can't send a reproducible example at the moment, so just looking for general advice for parallelizing nimble fits.

Thank you for your time,
Ann Raiho

messages.subject: Re: mclapply with nimble
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ann,

Check out this new NIMBLE example page on parallelizing <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/parallelizing_NIMBLE.html> for a sample we found to work. You may find it helpful.

I'm not sure about the issue of failing to load shared libraries you've described. In general,  the entire NIMBLE pipeline should be included in the parallelized code (e.g. not just the "run MCMC" step). That could be the source of the problem if multiple processes are accessing the same underlying model simultaneously.

Hope that helps,
Ben

messages.subject: nesting nimble lists
messages.body_plain:
Dear Nimble-Users

I'm sure this is simple, but I'm struggling.

I want to make a nimbleList where each element is also a nimbleList containing one integer scalar and a character vector of variable lengths.  For example, in R I can do this...

myList <- list(node1=list(n=3, someText=c("A", "B", "C")), node2=list(n=2, someText=c("D", "A")), node3=list(n=1, someText=c("B")))

But I want to be able to do this inside some setup code where the character vectors are obtained via iterative calls to  model$getDependencies(someNodes[iterationNumber]). Here n is the length of the character vector, which is defined by the DAG generated by a nimble model. I don't see how I can handle the different and unknown lengths returned by each call to getDependencies.

I could alternatively use modelValues instead, but I still don't see how to handle the mix of dimensions (character vector lengths).

Any thoughts?
David

messages.subject: Re: PMCMC samples of latent states
messages.body_plain:
Hi again

I'm having some trouble understanding how to scale my state space model for variable time intervals correctly.
basically the below model works, but only if dT = 1, if I change it to something closer to my real problem say 600. many of the samples for x[,1] end up being very very small, with low logProb of data node errors. Not quite sure what is wrong.

Example code:
require(nimble)
require(ggplot2)
require(data.table)

timeModelCode <- nimbleCode({
    # inital states
  x[1,1] ~ dnorm(y[1], sd = obs_error) # C
  x[1,2] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 5) # J
  x[1,3] ~ dnorm(kw[1] * (Csat - x[1,1]), sd = 0.0001) # gas exchange

    # state space evolution
  for(i in 2:t){
    x[i,1] ~ dnorm(x[i-1,1] + (x[i-1,2] * dT) + (x[i-1,3] * dT), sd = pro_error) # change in C
    x[i,2] ~ dnorm(x[i-1,2], sd = var_J) # J, (random walk)
    x[i,3] ~ dnorm(kw[i] * (Csat - x[i,1]), sd = 0.0001) # G
    y[i] ~ dnorm(x[i,1], sd = obs_error) # observation
  }

  obs_error ~ dnorm(0, sd=5)
  pro_error ~ dnorm(0, sd=1)
  var_J ~ dnorm(0, 1) # how much J varies between steps

})

# simulate some data

t <- 48
pro_error <- 0.1
obs_error <- 0.5
x <- rep(300, t) # inital state + populate vector
y <- rnorm(1, x, obs_error) # first observation
dT = 600 # time between observations (seconds)

J = (8 * sin(0.03 * pi * 1:t) + 0.5) / dT # our unobserved latent state of interest
kw = rep(3e-05, t)
Csat = 250
G = rep(0, t)
G[1] <- kw[1] * (Csat - x[1])

for(i in 2:t){
  x[i] <- x[i-1] + (J[i-1] * dT) + (G[i-1] * dT)
  G[i] <- rnorm(1, kw[i] * (Csat - x[i]), 0.0001)

  y[i] <- rnorm(1, x[i], obs_error)
}

truth = data.table(x, J, G, t = 1:t)
truth = melt(truth, id.vars = "t")
truth[, var := as.numeric(as.factor(variable))]

# y[10:20] = NA # for testing missing observations

plot(x, type="l")
points(y, col="red")

plot(J, type="l")
lines(G, col="blue")
plot(J + G, type="l", col="red")

# build the model
rTimeModel <- nimbleModel(timeModelCode, constants = list(t = t, dT = dT),
                          data <- list(y = y, kw = kw, Csat = Csat), check = T,
                          inits = list(var_J = 1, obs_error = 0.1, pro_error = 0.1)) # should x be init?
rTimeModel$initializeInfo()

cTimeModel <- compileNimble(rTimeModel)

timeConf <- configureMCMC(rTimeModel)

# Add random walk PMCMC sampler with particle number optimization.

timeConf$addSampler(target = c("var_J", "obs_error", "pro_error"), type = "RW_PF_block",
                    control <- list(pfType = "auxiliary", pfControl = list(saveAll = T, smoothing = T),
                                    latents = c("x")))

timeConf$addMonitors("x")
RtimeConf <- buildMCMC(timeConf)
CtimeConf <- compileNimble(RtimeConf, project=rTimeModel, resetFunctions=T)

CtimeConf$run(5000)

  # check top level parameters against truth
hist(as.matrix(CtimeConf$mvSamples, "obs_error"), breaks=100)
abline(v=obs_error, col="red")

hist(as.matrix(CtimeConf$mvSamples, "pro_error"), breaks=100)
abline(v=pro_error, col="red")

hist(as.matrix(CtimeConf$mvSamples, "var_J"), breaks=100)
abline(v=sd(diff(J)), col="red")

  # extract time series latent state samples, if there is more elegant way of doing this I don't know it.
out = as.matrix(CtimeConf$mvSamples, "x")
out = melt(data.table(out))
out = out[,.(mean = mean(value, na.rm = F), min= quantile(value, 0.05, na.rm=F), max=quantile(value, 0.95, na.rm=F)), by=variable]
out[, t := stringr::str_extract_all(variable, "\\d+", simplify = T)[,1]]
out[, var := stringr::str_extract_all(variable, "\\d+", simplify = T)[,2]]
out[, t := as.numeric(t)]
#
ggplot(out) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(t, ymin=min, ymax=max), alpha=0.5) +
  geom_point(data=truth, aes(t, value)) +
  facet_grid(var ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  geom_line(aes(t, mean))

messages.body_plain:
Cracked it! This does what I need.

#################
## Toy Example ##
#################
rm(list=ls())
library(nimble)

toyCode <- nimbleCode({
    rate[1,1] <- state[1,1]
    rate[2,1] <- state[1,1] + state[2,1] + state[3,1]
    rate[3,1] <- state[1,1] + state[2,1]
    rate[1,2] <- state[1,1] + state[2,2] + state[2,3]
    rate[2,2] <- state[1,1] + state[3,3]
    rate[3,2] <- state[1,1] + sum(state[3,])
})

inits    <- list(state = matrix(1:9, nrow=3))
toyModel <- nimbleModel(toyCode, inits=inits)
toyModel[["state"]]
toyModel[["rate"]]

(stateIndices <- as.vector(outer(1:dim(toyModel[["state"]])[1], 1:dim(toyModel[["state"]])[2], paste, sep=",")))
(stateNodes   <- paste0("state[",stateIndices,"]"))
(nStateNodes  <- length(stateNodes))
(stateIndices <- paste0("row",sub(",","col",stateIndices)))

(rateIndices <- as.vector(outer(1:dim(toyModel[["rate"]])[1], 1:dim(toyModel[["rate"]])[2], paste, sep=",")))
(rateNodes   <- paste0("rate[",rateIndices,"]"))
(nRateNodes  <- length(rateNodes))

## Define list structures
innerList <- nimbleList(n = integer(0), txt = character(1))
(outerDef  <- paste0("nimbleList(",paste0(stateIndices, "=innerList()", collapse=","),")"))
outerList <- eval(parse(text=outerDef))

## Create outer list
dependentRatesList <- outerList$new()

## Create inner list & fill outer list
for (iSN in 1:nStateNodes) { ## iSN=2
    (deps <- toyModel$getDependencies(stateNodes[iSN]))
    (deps <- deps[grep("rate", deps)])
    eval(parse(text=paste0("dependentRatesList$",stateIndices[iSN], " <- innerList$new(n=", length(deps),", txt=deps)")))
}

print(dependentRatesList)

messages.subject: Re: nesting nimble lists
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

Thanks for this.

Right, one nimbleList can contain elements whose type is a different nimbleList.

I understand the need for numeric indexing, and more flexibly data structures in general.  Here is another option.  You can treat a nimbleFunction with setup code as simply a data structure, since it yields a class definition.  In the setup code, "setupOutputs(my_var, my_other_var)" will ensure that "my_var" and "my_other_var" are established as member data of the resulting class definition.  You can then make a nimbleFunctionList of this nimbleFunction type, giving you a numerically-indexed list of objects with whatever types you created in setup code.  The easiest way to get the types you want is to create my_var and my_other_var in setup code as objects of the types you want.

This is a quick reply but we can dive deeper if it would help.

Best,
Perry

I haven't tried to run your code yet.  Could you say what the error messages are?  I'm not seeing them in your most recent emails.

The x values should be drawn by the particle filter, starting from the prior for x[1, 1:3].  So I wonder if there are bad initial values for the top-level parameters (obs_error, pro_error, var_J)?  It might help to set the prior for var_J to be only positive.

BTW, nimble 0.9-0 is released and has the updates to particle filtering methods mentioned by Chris earlier in this email thread.

-Perry

messages.subject: problem of initializing stochastic node
messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone,

I am presently working on a model to model demography and phenology of Bumblebees. The problem I have is that one of the stochastic nodes(K) in my model is not initializing, the log probabilities are -Inf.  For example, the error I get in nimble for one node point is warning: problem initializing stochastic node K[1, 8, 2]: logProb is -Inf.   K is a 2x30X3 array. and I have multiple warning messages. I've used initial values for K in nimbleModel and I've used model$calculate("K") and this results in -Inf.  I've read from a recent post,  that this may be that K  itself or something that K depends on may not be initialized well. I've checked and other nodes depending on K are not NA or  -Inf.   My question then is how to I initialized K well?

In addition, what are some guidelines for choosing starting values for stochastic nodes?

Many thanks for all the help,
Fabian

messages.subject: Re: problem of initializing stochastic node
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fabian,

A good strategy is to look at the nodes that K depends on, not the nodes that depend on K.

Here is an artificial example.  Say you have nodes

...
K ~ dnorm(mu, sd = sigma)
sigma ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
...

and you see that model$calculate("K") returns -Inf.

Typically that must mean that either mu or sigma is the problem.  Those are the nodes that K depends on.  You can look at them directly by:

model$mu
model$sigma
and also check K itself:
model$K

where "model" is what is returned from nimbleModel.

In this case, you might see that sigma is negative or NA, resulting in a problem for dnorm.  The solution would be to ensure a valid initial value for sigma, either by changing its prior or (better) providing a reasonable value in the inits.

HTH.  If that doesn't get you on the right path, please send a reproducible example.

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: nesting nimble lists
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

We know the User Manual is so long that it can sometimes be hard to find what you need. (That's one reason we made more examples for the web site recently, and of course we wish had time to do more, and we do welcome suggestions (or contributions) even if we don't always have time to take them up quickly.)  However, it is in there!  It's in section 15.4.10, "User-defined data structures".

Regarding assignment to non-scalar objects: You can change the sizes, but not the number of indices.  (Unfortunately the word "dimension" gets used in a couple of different ways in this context.)  For example, if X was already created as a matrix and A and B are matrices and C is a 3D array (i.e. an object with 3 indices), then:

X <- A %*% B ## OK: complete replacement of X; nimble compiler will manage the memory for you.
X <- C ## Error: can't assign a 3D object (having 3 indices) two a 2D (matrix) object.
X <- C[1:5, , 3] ## OK: complete replacement of X from a 2D object created by indexing a 3D object; nimble compiler will manage the memory for you.

HTH
-Perry

On Thu, Jan 16, 2020 at 12:33 AM 'David Pleydell' via nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> > Here is another option.  You can treat a nimbleFunction with setup code as simply a data structure, since it yields a class definition.  In the setup code, "setupOutputs(my_var, my_other_var)" will ensure that "my_var" and "my_other_var" are established as member data of the resulting class definition.  You can then make a nimbleFunctionList of this nimbleFunction type, giving you a numerically-indexed list of objects with whatever types you created in setup code.  The easiest way to get the types you want is to create my_var and my_other_var in setup code as objects of the types you want.
> >
> > This is a quick reply but we can dive deeper if it would help.
>
> Many thanks Perry,

> That certainly sounds like an interesting option - it would be great to see an example of that make either the manual or the website in the future. For now I can make do with the solution I found, so I'll stick with that.

In C this would require re-allocating memory, so would nimble handle that automatically, or would the user need to build a memory re-allocation step into their code ?

messages.body_plain:
Many thanks for the help guys. My model seems to be compiling well.  Here is where I had problems:

E ~ dmulti(betas, N)
K ~ dpois(E)

E can be greater and equal to zero and the issue was the logprob of K was -Inf when E=0 and K >0. Is there any other way to circumvent this issue other than creating a user-defined distribution to handle this case?

Cheers,
Fabian

On Thursday, 16 January 2020 17:55:48 UTC, Daniel Turek wrote:

>

> On Thu, Jan 16, 2020 at 6:41 PM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:

> > Hi Fabian,
> >
> > A good strategy is to look at the nodes that K depends on, not the nodes that depend on K.
> >
> > Here is an artificial example.  Say you have nodes
> >
> > ...
> > K ~ dnorm(mu, sd = sigma)
> > sigma ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
> > ...
> >
> > and you see that model$calculate("K") returns -Inf.
> >
> > Typically that must mean that either mu or sigma is the problem.  Those are the nodes that K depends on.  You can look at them directly by:
> >
> > model$mu
> > model$sigma
> > and also check K itself:
> > model$K
> >
> > where "model" is what is returned from nimbleModel.
> >
> > In this case, you might see that sigma is negative or NA, resulting in a problem for dnorm.  The solution would be to ensure a valid initial value for sigma, either by changing its prior or (better) providing a reasonable value in the inits.
> >
> > HTH.  If that doesn't get you on the right path, please send a reproducible example.
> >
> > -Perry

messages.subject: Re: problem of initializing stochastic node
messages.body_plain:
I didn't follow the whole threat, but the lambda parameter from the Poisson distribution cannot be equals to 0. However, E can be equals to 0, given it comes from a multinomial distribution. Doing something like
K ~ dpois(E +1)
is an ugly shortcut, but should suffice.

I also would like to add that I never saw a multinomial distribution being used as a prior for a Poisson distribution. messages.subject: 'Error: Failed to create the shared library' after updating to Catalina on MacOS
messages.subject_clean: 'Error: Failed to create the shared library' after updating to Catalina on MacOS
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was trying to run some code, and got the following error when using compileNimble(): "Error : Failed to create the shared library.". This code was working like a charm on my Mac before I updated to Catalina.

Using the 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE’ option produced more details which didn’t help though.

Fortunately for me, Daniel Turek who’s on sabbatical with us in Montpellier had a look and found these:

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58313047/cannot-compile-r-packages-with-c-code-after-updating-to-macos-catalina

https://thecoatlessprofessor.com/programming/cpp/r-compiler-tools-for-rcpp-on-macos/

To fix the issue, I had to simply run the following command from the OSX Terminal application and restart my laptop:

$ xcode-select --install

I thought I’d share my experience in case other Nimble users run into the same troubles.

Cheers, and thank you Daniel. Back to my Nimble experiments I guess :-) Thanks to the whole team for such an amazing work!

Olivier

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Dr Olivier Gimenez | senior scientist at CNRS
olivier...@cefe.cnrs.fr | https://oliviergimenez.github.io/

Due to my own family/work balance, you may get emails from
me outside of normal working hours. Please do not feel any
pressure to respond outside of your own working pattern.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

#################

#################

    rate[1,1] <- state[1,1]
    rate[2,1] <- state[1,1] + state[2,1] + state[3,1]

    rate[1,2] <- state[1,1] + state[1,2] + state[2,2] + state[3,2]
    rate[2,2] <- sum(state[,])
})

inits    <- list(state = matrix(1:6, nrow=3))

toyModel <- nimbleModel(toyCode, inits=inits)
toyModel[["state"]]
toyModel[["rate"]]

##########################################################

    setup = function(model, rateNode="rate", stateNode="state") {
        ## Obtain stateNodes, nStateNodes and stateIndices
        (stateIndices <- as.vector(outer(1:dim(model[[stateNode]])[1], 1:dim(model[[stateNode]])[2], paste, sep=",")))
        (stateNodes   <- paste0(stateNode,"[",stateIndices,"]"))

        (nStateNodes  <- length(stateNodes))
        (stateIndices <- paste0("row",sub(",","col",stateIndices)))

        ## Obtain rateIndices, rateNodes and nRateNodes
        (rateIndices  <- as.vector(outer(1:dim(model[[rateNode]])[1], 1:dim(model[[rateNode]])[2], paste, sep=",")))

            eval(parse(text=paste0("dependentRatesList$",stateIndices[iSN], " <- innerList$new(n=", length(deps),", txt=deps)")))

        ## Make objects available in run

    }
)

myFunc <- setupMyFunc(model=toyModel)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am a new convert to Nimble but I am struggling to transfer some CJS models from BUGS...

I have a similar problem to one posted the other day and I am trying to understand what is happening. I am trying to model survival/mortality from an extensive capture-mark-recapture dataset in a fairly simple CJS format, I have the model which runs in BUGS and I have been trying to reconfigure it to work in Nimble with some success but it repeatedly throws warning messages for every node (recapture event) that follows a zero in the capture history... so for example an individual capture history maybe 11101 to describe an individual who was captured on the first three possible occasions then not captured and then finally recaptured on the final occasion.  All seems to work ok but I get a warning saying warning: problem initializing stochastic node x[1, 5]: logProb is -Inf. So I am wondering waht is happening to throw this warning.  I think it is to do with my x_init values but not quite sure what they should in this situation.  I also tried this with the dipper model from Turek 2016 and had the same warning when I changed an individual's capture history to include a missed capture event.
I can add examples if need be but I think I am missing something simple!?
Many thanks,
Dave
So

## Latent State MCMC for the dipper model

x_init[1,4]<-0  #Create the missed capture event

## define hierarchical model
  code <- nimbleCode({
  phi ~ dunif(0, 1)
  p ~ dunif(0, 1)
  for (i in 1:nind) {
    x[i, first[i]] <- 1
    for (t in (first[i] + 1):k) {
      mu_x[i, t] <- phi * x[i, t-1]
      mu_y[i, t] <- p * x[i, t]
      x[i, t] ~ dbin(mu_x[i, t], 1)
      y[i, t] ~ dbin(mu_y[i, t], 1)
    }

})

## specify MCMC algorithm
spec <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
spec$printSamplers()

## build MCMC algorithm
Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(spec)

## compile model and MCMC
Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

## run MCMC
set.seed(0)
Cmcmc$run(10000)

messages.body_plain:
Yes, the issue is that when you "Create the missed capture event" as:

x_init[1,4]<-0  #Create the missed capture event

Then that initial value of x[1,4]=0 is inconsistent with the first row of the observation history:

> head(y)
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] [,7]
[1,]    1    1    1    1    1    1    0

Specifically, that y[1,4] = 1.  So x[1,4]=0 is an impossible initial value, since it can't give rise to the observation that takes place.

What again are you trying to accomplish, by setting x[1,4]=0 ?  There's most likely a different, more correct way of doing it.

Yes, I think this would be because a latent alive/dead history such as:
x[1, 1:7] = 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1

Implies that individual #1 was alive at T=1,2,3, then died in time period T=4, then came back to life in time period T=5, which is not possible.  So, that's the cause of that error.

I'm so sorry to not be following, but I'm still not sure what you mean by trying to induce "a missed capture event" ?  Do you perhaps mean one of the observation's one of the y[i,j]'s, should be changed to 0?

messages.body_plain:
I think what is needed for each initial state sequence to be some 1s followed by some 0s (or perhaps just all 1s).  Then there will be no initial states that represent an individual going from dead to alive.  In addition, the 1s in the initial states should extend at least as far in time as the last 1 in the corresponding capture history.  Then there will be no captures of dead individuals.  Initial states that represent dead to alive transitions or captures of dead individuals seem to be the most likely culprits for log probabilities of -Inf from the initial values.

To use your example:

y[1,] <- 1 1 1 0 1 1 0

I think a valid sequence of initial values for the alive/dead states would be
and x_init[1,] <- 1 1 1 1 1 1 0
where the last value could alternatively be 1.

dbern(p) is an alternative to dbin(p, 1)

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: nesting nimble lists
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

You're running into limitations of the nimbleList system.  It's not very general.

Typically, there is little to no dynamic run-time resolution of name-based indexing in compiled code.  Name-based indexing (e.g. model[[target]], where target is character) mostly works only if target is fixed in setup code and then baked in to the compiled code.  There are exceptions with vectors of node names, such as model$calculate(nodes[i]).  But your stateIndices is a character vector.  The reason something like " n   <- dependentRatesList[[stateIndices[iSN]]]$n" is not amenable to the compilation system is that the type of the result wouldn't be able to be determined at compile time, and there is no dynamic typing in compiled code.

Can you convey a more general picture of what you want to accomplish?  Do you want the "txt" entries to be used in model calculations and such, or for some other purpose?  My guess is that a nimbleFunctionList might work, or that a re-arrangement in what is managed in R vs. compiled nimbleFunctions could make sense, or possibly that what you want to do is beyond nimble's compilation system.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Actually, what I think you want to do is set x[1,] as *data* equal to 1 1 1 1 1 1 NA. Then the MCMC will not spin its wheels trying to update the first six states because they are essentially known to be 1.  The NA "missing data" means that element will be sampled.  Then I think you want to set x_init [1,] to NA NA NA NA NA NA [0 or 1 or NA].  The first six NAs are because you don't want to provide initial values for non-missing data nodes.  The last value could be 0, or 1, or NA (will be simulated from the prior).  Often in nimble it is a good idea to proactively provide good initial values instead of relying on draws from priors, but in this case it might not matter much.

In my previous answer I was focused on untangling the confusion about valid states and so was not thinking of the way you can set some unobserved states as de facto data in a model like this.

-Perry

      # Likelihood

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dave,

That's correct: One variable can contain data nodes and non-data nodes.  When providing data values for a variable, entries for the non-data elements should be NA.  One can then provide inits for the non-data elements. That's all similar to JAGS.

When initial values are not provided, they are drawn from their prior.  In your case, the data nodes for some x[i,] will be a series of 1s.  My point about the initial value for the first non-data node after the last 1 (i.e. after the time of last capture) is that you should at least get a valid value whether you make it 0 (the individual died), 1 (the individual survived) or NA (initial 0 or 1 will be drawn based on the survival probability).

One reason to provide a 0 or a 1 instead of an NA as inits is that using NA will trigger the warning that the model is not fully initialized (because it's not, which isn't necessarily a bad thing).  Another strategy is you can do model$simulate() to generate values everywhere, then model$calculate().  If the latter returns NA or -Inf, something is still not validly initialized.  As noted in the error message, having a not-fully-initialized model is not a bug or necessarily a problem.  The MCMC (or other algorithm, but I assume you are going for MCMC) might successfully initialize it.

The process for determining where you have some invalid initial value in the more complex model would be similar to what we've discussed so far.  You can control which parts of the model are calculated and you can look directly at variables and their associated log probability values, so the process is essentially one of digging around.  The steps are roughly as follows:

If model$calculate() is -Inf, try checking different parts of the model to see where something has log probability of -Inf.

e.g., model$calculate('z') will calculate the sum of log probabilities for all the z's.  model$calculate('z[1,]') will calculate for just z[1,],  etc.

When you have it narrowed down, such as if model$calculate('z') is -Inf, you can also look directly as each node's log probability with model$logProb_z

Then you can inspect values relevant to the calculation, e.g. inspect
model$z[1,]
model$phi[1,]
model$mu1
etc.
Usually this reveals values that result in a -Inf log probability, such as if a parameter to a distribution does not make sense.

HTH.  If you're still stuck, please send a reproducible example of the more complex model.
-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry,

Still having trouble with the various warnings when using the more complicated model and I am wondering whether it is an issue of identifiability, I have been using a very simplified data set to try and debug the code as you will see below....
Basically it is looking at mortality using the Siler function which describes age specific mortality through 5 parameters (a1,a2,b1,b2,c - and c has its lower bound which is dependent on some of the other parameters).  This code has worked in WinBUGS but it takes a long time!
Any thoughts would be very gratefully received!

Many thanks
Dave

#Set up matrices for capture history, known latent states, initial latent states and age (3 individuals, 6 time occasions)
Tch<- matrix(data = NA, nrow = 3, ncol = 6)
Tch[1,]<- c(1,1,0,1,0,0)
Tch[2,]<- c(1,0,0,1,1,1)
Tch[3,]<- c(1,0,0,1,1,0)

Tknown <- Tch
Tknown[1,]<- c(1,1,1,1,NA,NA)
Tknown[2,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,1)
Tknown[3,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,NA)

Tinit<- Tch
Tinit[1,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,1)
Tinit[2,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,1)
Tinit[3,]<- c(1,1,1,1,1,NA)

Tage<- Tch
Tage[1,]<- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
Tage[2,]<- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
Tage[3,]<- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)

Tf<- c(1,1,1)

CJS.code<- nimbleCode({
      # CJS Siler model with constrained C parameter for NIMBLE:
      # Priors and constraints

    for (i in 1:nind){

      for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){
        phi[i,t] <- exp((exp(a1)/b1)*(exp(-b1*x[i,t])-1) - c*x[i,t] + (exp(a2)/b2)*(1-exp(b2*x[i,t])))
        p[i,t] <- mean.p
      } #t
    } #i

    cl <- -exp(a1-(b1*xl)) - exp(a2-(b2*xl)) #Constrain c parameter
    xl <- (log(b1)+a1-log(b2)-a2)/(b1+b2)    #Constrain c parameter

    a1 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    b1 ~ dexp(0.1)
    a2 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    b2 ~ dexp(0.1)
    c ~ dunif(cl,10)
    mean.p ~ dunif(0,1)

      # Likelihood
    for (i in 1:nind){
      # Define latent state at first capture
      z[i,f[i]] <- 1
      for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){
        # State process
        z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])
        mu1[i,t] <- phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1]
        # Observation process
        y[i,t] ~ dbern(mu2[i,t])
        mu2[i,t] <- p[i,t-1] * z[i,t]
      } #t
    } #i
  })

CJS.Consts <- list(f=Tf, nind=3, n.occasions=6, x=Tage)
CJS.data <- list(y=Tch, z=Tknown)
CJS.inits <- list(
  z = Tinit,
  a1 = rnorm(1),
  a2 = rnorm(1),
  b1 = rexp(1, 0.1),
  b2 = rexp(1, 0.1),
  mean.p = runif(1,0,1),
  c = runif(1,1,10)
)

CJS<- nimbleModel(code=CJS.code, name = "CJS", constants = CJS.Consts,
                  data = CJS.data, inits = CJS.inits)

spec <- configureMCMC(CJS)
spec$printSamplers()

rMCMC<- buildMCMC(spec)

cCJS<- compileNimble(CJS)
cMCMC<- compileNimble(rCJS, project = CJS)

set.seed(0)
cMCMC$run(1000)

On Friday, 24 January 2020 17:14:22 UTC, pdevalpine wrote:

> Hi Dave,
>
> That's correct: One variable can contain data nodes and non-data nodes.  When providing data values for a variable, entries for the non-data elements should be NA.  One can then provide inits for the non-data elements. That's all similar to JAGS.
>
> When initial values are not provided, they are drawn from their prior.  In your case, the data nodes for some x[i,] will be a series of 1s.  My point about the initial value for the first non-data node after the last 1 (i.e. after the time of last capture) is that you should at least get a valid value whether you make it 0 (the individual died), 1 (the individual survived) or NA (initial 0 or 1 will be drawn based on the survival probability).
>
> One reason to provide a 0 or a 1 instead of an NA as inits is that using NA will trigger the warning that the model is not fully initialized (because it's not, which isn't necessarily a bad thing).  Another strategy is you can do model$simulate() to generate values everywhere, then model$calculate().  If the latter returns NA or -Inf, something is still not validly initialized.  As noted in the error message, having a not-fully-initialized model is not a bug or necessarily a problem.  The MCMC (or other algorithm, but I assume you are going for MCMC) might successfully initialize it.
>
> The process for determining where you have some invalid initial value in the more complex model would be similar to what we've discussed so far.  You can control which parts of the model are calculated and you can look directly at variables and their associated log probability values, so the process is essentially one of digging around.  The steps are roughly as follows:
>
> If model$calculate() is -Inf, try checking different parts of the model to see where something has log probability of -Inf.
>
> e.g., model$calculate('z') will calculate the sum of log probabilities for all the z's.  model$calculate('z[1,]') will calculate for just z[1,],  etc.
>
> When you have it narrowed down, such as if model$calculate('z') is -Inf, you can also look directly as each node's log probability with model$logProb_z
>
> Then you can inspect values relevant to the calculation, e.g. inspect
> model$z[1,]
> model$phi[1,]
> model$mu1
> etc.
> Usually this reveals values that result in a -Inf log probability, such as if a parameter to a distribution does not make sense.
>
> HTH.  If you're still stuck, please send a reproducible example of the more complex model.
> -Perry

messages.subject: WAIC comment page 85 Nimble manual 0.8.0
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I just started to use Nimble (a couple of days ago) and was reading through the manual and trying out some of the elementary features of the package.
First I want to say that I very much like the package. It appears that it extends the capabilities of standard BUGS software considerably.
But I have a problem understanding the meaning and the usefulness of computing WAIC on only the top-level nodes.
To compute WAIC, one needs to compute the full likelihood using all nodes, so what and how can one compute WAIC if the thetas are not monitored. What is computed then?
I tested this on a simple 2-level hierarchical model, first monitoring all stochastic nodes and then i did not explicitly monitor any parameters.
The example consists of cholesterol intakes in 8 centers, with latent means theta_i (i=1, ..., 8) and individual Gaussian data y_ij, with individual SD all equal to sigma.
The theta's have a Gaussian distribution with mean mu and SD = sigma_theta.
So, in the first case I monitored mu, sigma.theta, the theta's, sigma and then I got WAIC=6991, when I did not explicitly monitore any parameter (then Nimble monitors only mu and sigma.theta), then WAIC=7045.
Now I have difficulties to see what expression is used in the second case, and what the usefulness of this calculation.

Any help to get insight is welcome.

Emmanuel Lesaffre

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am encountering compilation errors when multiple nimbleFunctionLists share the same "contains" argument within a single setup function.  If I duplicate the nimbleFunctionVirtual code and create multiple names for essentially the same thing then my code compiles and runs as expected. If I remove the apparently redundant calls to nimbleFunctionVirtual my code will not compile.  My understanding (based on section 15.4.8 of the manual) is that the call to nimbleFunctionVirtual creates a class definition, so it does not make sense to me that two nimbleFunctionLists should not be able to share the same class definition.

My operating system is Ubuntu 18.04.3 LTS (Bionic Beaver).

I attach some code that compiles and runs fine as it is. To obtain the compiler error simply search for all instances of "Out2" and replace with "Out".  This results in the function lists "getState" and "getDeriv" sharing the same class definition (classVoidInDouble0Out) and the compiler does not accept that.

There are more explanations of what my code actually does in the header of the attached file. Please also let me know if you think the algorithm I've developed here is worthy of incorporation into nimble, or would be better released as a separate package.

If this is not a bug in nimble then a clearer error message would be a very valuable development.  The error message says "duplicate symbol name: getState", so I checked many times and found no duplication of getState. The problem was that I was using classVoidInDouble0Out multiple times, so an error message pointing to illegal recycling of classVoidInDouble0Out (and not getState) would have really helped.  It took me several days of blind stumbling before I hit on the Out2 solution.

Many thanks for continuing the nimble development. It's really a great tool!

All the best
David

messages.subject: Re: WAIC comment page 85 Nimble manual 0.8.0
messages.body_plain:
hi Emmanuel,

If you do not monitor all stochastic nodes, NIMBLE will simulate them conditional on the  posterior samples for the nodes you do monitor (but not conditional on any child nodes, such as the data). For example if you don't monitor your theta_i latent means, then NIMBLE  will simulate theta_i based on the posterior for the parameters that govern the theta_i values (mu and sigma_theta). In turn the predictive distribution for the observations will be calculated based on the theta_i that have just been simulated rather than the posterior samples of theta_i from the MCMC.

I think Section 2.5 of the Gelman et al. WAIC reference does a nice job of saying why one might want to simulate theta_i rather than conditioning on the posterior samples of theta_i.

Some notes along the lines of what I just said can be found via `help(buildMCMC)`, as can the full citation for the Gelman et al. paper.

-Chris

I'm getting some strange behavior with dinterval in a nimble model.

Here's the relevant code in the nimble model:

# Likelihood
for (n in 1:N) {
   prob[n, 1:time_steps] <- ilogit(X[n, , ] %*% Beta[])
   censored[n] ~ dinterval(z[n], y[n, 1:2])
   z[n] ~ dtvgeom_nimble(prob[n, 1:time_steps])

   y_rep[n] ~ dtvgeom_nimble(prob[n, 1:time_steps])
}

dtvgeom_nimble is registered as a discrete distribution:

registerDistributions(list(
  dtvgeom_nimble = list(
    BUGSdist = "dtvgeom_nimble(prob)",
    pqAvail = TRUE,
    discrete = TRUE,
    range = c(1, Inf),
    types = c("prob = double(1)")
  )), verbose = F, userEnv = .GlobalEnv)

When I monitor z in the output, I'm seeing non-integer values. Monitoring y_rep shows (correctly) integer values only, so I'm assuming it must have something to do with invoking dinterval. Any idea what might be going on?

Thanks for any insight!

- Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hmm, it looks like there may be a bug related to types somewhat deep in our compilation system where we check that the lengths of the vectors you are subtracting are the same.

As a work-around, please try this:

1) Add this just before your loops:
idx1 <- 2:(TT-1)
idx2 <- 1:(TT-2)

2) Then use 'idx1' and 'idx2' in the main line with the calls to pnorm():

 betas[y, ,c] <- c(pnorm(1, mu[c], sigma[c]), pnorm(idx1, mu[c], sigma[c]) - pnorm(idx2, mu[c], sigma[c]), 1 - pnorm(TT-1, mu[c], sigma[c]))

I will come up with a smaller reproducible example and file as a bug report for us to look at.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Op donderdag 30 januari 2020 02:39:27 UTC+1 schreef Chris Paciorek:

> hi Emmanuel,
>
> If you do not monitor all stochastic nodes, NIMBLE will simulate them conditional on the  posterior samples for the nodes you do monitor (but not conditional on any child nodes, such as the data). For example if you don't monitor your theta_i latent means, then NIMBLE  will simulate theta_i based on the posterior for the parameters that govern the theta_i values (mu and sigma_theta). In turn the predictive distribution for the observations will be calculated based on the theta_i that have just been simulated rather than the posterior samples of theta_i from the MCMC.
>
> I think Section 2.5 of the Gelman et al. WAIC reference does a nice job of saying why one might want to simulate theta_i rather than conditioning on the posterior samples of theta_i.
>
> Some notes along the lines of what I just said can be found via `help(buildMCMC)`, as can the full citation for the Gelman et al. paper.
>
> -Chris
>
>

> On Tue, Jan 28, 2020 at 10:57 AM Emmanuel Lesaffre <e.lesa...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Hi all,
> > I just started to use Nimble (a couple of days ago) and was reading through the manual and trying out some of the elementary features of the package.
> > First I want to say that I very much like the package. It appears that it extends the capabilities of standard BUGS software considerably.
> > But I have a problem understanding the meaning and the usefulness of computing WAIC on only the top-level nodes.
> > To compute WAIC, one needs to compute the full likelihood using all nodes, so what and how can one compute WAIC if the thetas are not monitored. What is computed then?
> > I tested this on a simple 2-level hierarchical model, first monitoring all stochastic nodes and then i did not explicitly monitor any parameters.
> > The example consists of cholesterol intakes in 8 centers, with latent means theta_i (i=1, ..., 8) and individual Gaussian data y_ij, with individual SD all equal to sigma.
> > The theta's have a Gaussian distribution with mean mu and SD = sigma_theta.
> > So, in the first case I monitored mu, sigma.theta, the theta's, sigma and then I got WAIC=6991, when I did not explicitly monitore any parameter (then Nimble monitors only mu and sigma.theta), then WAIC=7045.
> > Now I have difficulties to see what expression is used in the second case, and what the usefulness of this calculation.
> >
> > Any help to get insight is welcome.
> >
> > Emmanuel Lesaffre

messages.body_plain:
Vincent, this was an interesting investigation.

I wish I had a better understanding of the internals of the doParallel package, and similarly foreach.  But I can confirm that with your current code, when the multiple (>1) workers are instantiated and deployed using makeCluster() and registerDoParallel(), those instances are not finding the distribution registration that you did earlier.  As a result, in each instance, a (normally default) RW sampler is being assigned to each z[], thus giving rise to non-integer samples.

I tried another approach, and put the registerDistributions() call inside the foreach() call, inside your definition of the tempo_mcmc() function.  The (very simply) modified code is below.  I checked that now slice samplers were assigned to the z[]'s, which is nimble's default sampler for discrete-valued latent states.  Indeed, now it works as intended, and the posterior samples for the z[]'s are all integer-valued.  So I think this fixes your problem.

There are certainly some interesting questions here about scoping and interplay between packages.  But barring those, I hope the code below will get you moving again.

Cheers, and thanks for your use and interest in nimble,
Daniel

out <- foreach(i = 1:n_chains,
               .combine = list,
               .packages = c("nimble", "tempo"),
               .multicombine = TRUE) %dopar% {
                   pheno_model <- suppressMessages(
                       nimbleModel(code = eval(parse(text = tempo:::nimble_model(beta_random_indices,
                                                         correlated))),
                                   name = "pheno",
                                   constants = inputs$pheno_consts,
                                   data = inputs$pheno_data,
                                   inits = inputs$pheno_inits # TODO: [[i]] # different inits for each chain
                                   )
                   )
                   suppressWarnings(registerDistributions(list(

                       dtvgeom_nimble = list(
                           BUGSdist = "dtvgeom_nimble(prob)",
                           pqAvail = TRUE,
                           discrete = TRUE,
                           range = c(1, Inf),
                           types = c("prob = double(1)")

                       )), verbose = F, userEnv = .GlobalEnv))
                   mcmc_cfg <- configureMCMC(pheno_model,
                                             monitors = monitors)
                   samp <- mcmc_cfg$getSamplers()
                   pheno_mcmc <- buildMCMC(mcmc_cfg)
                   compiled_mcmc <- suppressMessages(compileNimble(pheno_model,
                                                                   pheno_mcmc))
                   out_temp <- runMCMC(compiled_mcmc$pheno_mcmc,
                                       niter = n_iter + n_burnin,
                                       nburnin = n_burnin)
                   return(list(out_temp, samp))
               }
stopCluster(cl)
